newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco sees deficit, inflation at 3.0 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Morocco sees deficit, inflation at 3.0 pct in 1997.

text.p: Morocco sees a budget deficit and inflation of around 3.0 percent in 1997, nearly the same as 1996, Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj said on Wednesday.
Briefing reporters on the country's economic situation, Kabbaj said good agricultural results were behind the improvement in 1996 and the good prospects of 1997.
"We expect, with God willing, the budget deficit and inflation to be kept under control around 3.0 percent in 1997, or nearly the same in 1996," Kabbaj said.

The 3.0 percent budget deficit is equivalent to 9.6 billion dirhams, the minister said. The inflation was at 6.1 percent in 1995, while the budget deficit was at 4.7 percent in 1995 due to the negative effects of the drought.

Kabbaj, who took part in a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali, said Morocco posted gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 11.8 percent in 1996 and would register between 3.0 to 4.0 percent growth in 1997.
The trade balance was down 13.5 percent in 1996 compared with 1995. The payment balance posted a 3.0 billion dirhams surplus in 1996 after a 7.3 billion deficit in 1995.
Ordinary tax receipts rose 11.3 percent compared with 1995 and national savings rose to 19 percent of GDP against 16 percent in 1995.
"Due to these positive factors, Morocco's foreign reserves rose to $4.0 billion in 1996, up $328 million over the previous year...This represents more than six months imports," Kabbaj said.
Privatisation receipts are expected to drop to 4.0 billion dirhams ($436.6 million) instead of 5.0 billion dirhams ($546 million) scheduled earlier for the fiscal year ending in June 1997.
Foreign debt represented 60 percent of GDP in 1996 against 68 percent in 1995.
"Morocco's total debt is estimated at $21 billion, of which the Treasury holds a stake of $14 billion," he said. He forescast the debt would drop to 40 percent of GDP by 2000.
Kabbaj said Morocco hired J.P. Morgan to rate Morocco's economic sectors.
"We expect the final results for the rating of the Moroccan economy to be issued by June 1997," he said.
To stimulate the T-bond market, the government also plans to cut interest rates on the Treasury bonds listed on the stock exchange in March 1997, Kabbaj added without further details.
